title: Chapter 1 knowledge graph: concepts, prerequisites, parallels, misconceptions
version: 3.9 (coverage audit; six node types; ways are has_level edge logic)
source: R. Sedgewick and K. Wayne, Introduction to Programming in Java, 1st ed. (2008), Chapter 1 (Sections 1.1-1.6), checked page by page; A. B. Downey and C. Mayfield, Think Java, 2nd ed. (2020), for what S&W Chapter 1 does not cover

schema.description: Chapter 1 knowledge graph (Sedgewick & Wayne, Introduction to Programming in Java, 1.1-1.6), checked against the 1st-ed. book (2008) and Think Java 2nd ed. Six node types: section, topic, concept, misconception, error, learning level. Each concept has its 5 learning-progression levels (L0-L4) attached by has_level edges; the edge logic of a has_level edge states the ways of reaching that level (each way has its edge_logic: the exact rule of the concept that the way tests, of one of 13 rule categories; exact_rule holds the same text). Ways are edge logic, not nodes. concept.rules_by_type holds all 13 rule categories with verified sources.

learning_levels.attachment: every concept has 5 learning_level nodes (L0-L4), attached by has_level edges. The level node holds the level, its name, the criterion statement and the deciding question; the has_level edge logic holds the ways of reaching it (edge.ways, one entry per way)

L0.everyday_reading.quote: This analogy is conversing with a human
L0.everyday_reading.note: Names the everyday source of meaning novices read into code: human conversation.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: may be described as the idea that there is a hidden mind somewhere in the programming language that
L0.everyday_reading.note: Pea's superbug: code is read as if an intelligent listener interprets it; the root of L0 everyday reading.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: because programming is a formal system that interprets each part
L0.everyday_reading.note: Edge to L1+: correct reading treats each part as interpreted by mechanistic rules, not by conversational pragmatics.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: they act as if the programming language is more than mechanistic
L0.everyday_reading.note: Observable sign: behaviour contradicts students' own denial that the computer thinks.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: novice prograninicrs often utilize intentional terms
L0.everyday_reading.note: Diagnostic cue: intentional vocabulary ('wants to', 'is waiting for') when describing execution.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: This is a remnant of the sensorimotor stage, where the language in the domain is still developing.
L0.everyday_reading.note: Reading every token verbatim ('console dot writeline') marks a sensorimotor reader still without domain language.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: In terms of reading and understanding a small piece of code, a student who gives a prestructural response is manifesting either a significant misconception of programming, or is using a preconception that is irrelevant to programming.
L0.everyday_reading.note: SOLO prestructural splits into two routes: an irrelevant (everyday) preconception -> everyday_reading, or a programming misconception -> misconception.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: Prestructural Substantially lacks knowledge of programming constructs or is unrelated to the question
L0.everyday_reading.note: Whalley's SOLO table (reproduced): prestructural = lacks construct knowledge or answer unrelated to the question.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: Shows no understanding of the code beyond that it is a collection of statements
L0.everyday_reading.note: Score 0 descriptor: recognises only that the text is code; no working model of what it does.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: English transliterations of statements in the code), but shows almost no ability
L0.everyday_reading.note: Boundary L0 vs L1/L2: reading the statements aloud in English (transliteration) is still score 0 if behaviour is not interpreted; true statements alone do not lift an answer out of L0.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: A prestructural response manifests either a significant misconception of programming or a preconception that is irrelevant to programming.
L0.everyday_reading.note: SOLO prestructural has two sources: a programming misconception (L0.misconception) or a preconception irrelevant to programming (L0.everyday_reading).

L0.everyday_reading.quote: The student lacks knowledge of programming constructs and approaches the task under study in a non appropriate or unrelated way.
L0.everyday_reading.note: Observable L0 behaviour: an approach unrelated to the programming constructs in the task.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: The response has little or no relevance to the given task or problem
L0.everyday_reading.note: Table 1 prestructural descriptor (arrays paper); first of three bullets.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: Substantial lack of knowledge in terms of the programming constructs involved
In our context this would mean categorizing according to the origins of students' errors, e.g. misconceptions from natural language, everyday life or math education.
L0.everyday_reading.note: Names natural language, everyday life and maths as sources of wrong readings; this is what everyday_reading looks for.
Natural-language reading as a named conceptual error class: the everyday_reading source.

L0.everyday_reading.quote: Often students hold conceptions that may be incorrect in a given PL, but that would reasonably hold in a different (existing or potential) language.
L0.everyday_reading.note: Prior-language or other-language readings as a source of L0 answers.

L0.misconception.quote: It is at this stage that misconceptions about basic programming concepts most influence the novice's behaviour
L0.misconception.note: Places holding documented wrong rules at the sensorimotor stage (L0).

L0.misconception.quote: The best known problems faced by novices at this level are misconceptions about the semantics of programming language constructs.
L0.misconception.note: Pre-tracing (sensorimotor) stage defined by misconceptions about construct semantics.

L0.misconception.quote: the preoperational novice has made headway into mastering basic programming concepts, with most misconceptions having now been rectified
L0.misconception.note: Edge L0->L2: misconceptions largely gone is the entry condition for preoperational tracing.

L0.misconception.quote: These errors are bugs in the sense that they are systematic-that is, n o t random crrors o r sloppy work
L0.misconception.note: Criterion separating a misconception (systematic wrong rule) from a slip.

L0.misconception.quote: In terms of reading and understanding a small piece of code, a student who gives a prestructural response is manifesting either a significant misconception of programming, or is using a preconception that is irrelevant to programming.
L0.misconception.note: Holding a significant programming misconception is by definition a prestructural (L0) response.

L0.misconception.quote: In this study, we also see few comprehension errors due to misconceptions.
L0.misconception.note: Most wrong answers came from fragile tracing, not construct misconceptions - L0 misconception is the rarer route here.

L0.misconception.quote: Among the top 75% of students, in all but one question, there is little evidence of construct misconceptions.
L0.misconception.note: Construct misconceptions concentrated in Q6 (return) and in bottom-quartile students.

L0.misconception.quote: Significant programming misconception
L0.misconception.note: Table 1: a significant misconception is a prestructural marker.

L0.misconception.quote: a "misconception" is a specific kind of difficulty that is based in a concrete mental model about a specific programming concept that does not align with reality or widely accepted scientific notions
L0.misconception.note: Misconception = a concrete but wrong mental model of one concept; this is what the L0 misconception way detects.

L0.misconception.quote: In order to have a misconception students need to have some form of understanding of a concept even though it is incorrect or deficient.
L0.misconception.note: Separates misconception (a wrong but present model) from everyday_reading (no model of the construct).

L0.misconception.quote: This means that we do not include syntactic or lexical errors as we consider them to be fundamentally different in nature.
L0.misconception.note: Syntactic slips are not conceptual misconceptions; they should not by themselves put an answer at L0 misconception.

L0.misconception.quote: in the case of C (mismatched brackets), a syntax error, this is likely to be an easy accident, but in the case of I (wrong types in method call) and O (missing return statement) this is more likely to be a lack of understanding or difficulty with the concepts of types and control flow.
L0.misconception.note: Repetition per user separates slips (accident) from a lack of understanding (misconception).

L0.misconception.quote: We refer in this paper to mistakes, and do not seek to distinguish between misconceptions (longstanding confusion) and slips (occasional mistakes).
L0.misconception.note: Blackbox mistakes are not all misconceptions; a single mistake is not by itself L0 misconception evidence.

L0.misconception.quote: How many times must one user make a mistake before it is considered a misconception rather than a slip?
L0.misconception.note: The open boundary between slip and misconception.

L0.misconception.quote: If educators talked about programming features at a higher level (e.g. the conceptual difficulties that students have with looping or variables) then we might find more of a consensus than when looking at specific syntax and semantic mistakes.
L0.misconception.note: Supports grouping surface mistakes under conceptual misconception nodes per concept.

L0.misconception.quote: Definition 2.1. A programming language misconception is a statement that can be disproved by reasoning entirely based on the syntax and/or semantics of a programming language.
L0.misconception.note: The misconception way definition: the wrong idea is a statement the language spec can refute.

L0.misconception.quote: Smith et al. [34], analyzing research in science and mathematics education, characterize misconceptions as "student conceptions that produce a systematic pattern of errors".
L0.misconception.note: Systematic (repeated) errors = misconception, vs single slips.

L0.misconception.quote: Sorva [38] defines them as "understandings that are deficient or inadequate for many practical programming contexts".
L0.misconception.note: Broader definition.

L0.misconception.quote: For each misconception we provide a description of the corresponding correct conception.
L0.misconception.note: Refutation form: wrong statement + correct conception; matches the way template "{wrong} contradicts {right}".

L0.misconception.quote: Both the shorter statement and the longer description represent the wrong conception: they violate in some way the associated PL's syntax and/or semantics.
L0.misconception.note: The statement is the wrong rule itself.

L0.misconception.quote: Some statements describe something students do rather than a belief they have about the syntax or semantics of a language. They are not themselves misconceptions but may be symptoms of a misconception, which would require further investigation to determine.
L0.misconception.note: An error (something done) is not a misconception (a belief); it is evidence to diagnose.

L0.misconception.quote: Statements about students' difficulties, although valuable teaching information, are also not programming language misconceptions according to our definition.
L0.misconception.note: Difficulties are not misconception nodes.

L0.misconception.quote: Some statements refer not to knowledge about a programming language but to strategic knowledge about programming in general.
L0.misconception.note: Strategic/design beliefs are out of scope.

L0.misconception.quote: Analyzing Sorva's list of misconceptions, we see that 70% of misconceptions fulfill our definition
L0.misconception.note: 70% of Sorva catalogue fit.

L0.misconception.quote: However, definitions broader than ours make it more difficult to clearly delineate the boundary between misconceptions and difficulties in general.
L0.misconception.note: Why a narrow definition.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: At this stage the novice requires considerable effort to trace code (i.e., hand execute), and only occasionally do they manage to do so accurately.
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Sensorimotor tracing is only occasionally accurate: the basis of an inconsistent trace at L0.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: Students who trace code with less than 50% accuracy are operating at a lower Piagetian level than preoperational, which is called the sensorimotor level
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Quantitative edge L0/L2: tracing accuracy below 50% = sensorimotor.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: There also exist other problems, which result in the novice being unable to accurately trace (i.e. manually execute) small pieces of code
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Pre-tracing stage: cannot accurately trace small code.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: Charlotte is manifesting behaviours of both the sensorimotor and preoperational stages.
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Overlapping waves: mixed correct and incorrect traces within one session.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: A sensorimotor novice finds any tracing task to be non-trivial and for that reason is reluctant to do so more than the minimum necessary.
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Behavioural cue of L0 tracing: reluctance to retrace.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: where a person exhibits characteristics from two or more stages as they develop skills in the domain
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Overlapping-waves model justifies a level for answers mixing correct and wrong rule use.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: Many of the students manifested a fragile ability to systematically analyze a short piece of code.
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Conclusion: fragility (sometimes-right) is the dominant weakness.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: Students can hold semi-correct or multiple (correct or incorrect) notions of a concept at the same time.
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Direct basis for inconsistent_trace: correct and wrong notions coexist and surface at different points of one trace.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: Especially in programming where novice students usually have little to no prior knowledge misconceptions can be fragile knowledge held by the students trying to make some sense of a program, as opposed to firm believes about a concept
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Fragile (unstable) wrong knowledge is the inconsistent_trace case; a stable wrong rule is the misconception case.

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: This can be a clear misconception, fragile knowledge or just a description of how students struggle with the concept.
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Three grades of L0 evidence: clear misconception (misconception way), fragile knowledge (inconsistent_trace), general struggle (no node).

L0.inconsistent_trace.quote: Like facets, our statements "describe students' thinking as it is seen or heard in the classroom", and they are "individual pieces or constructions of a few pieces of knowledge" [24].
L0.inconsistent_trace.note: Knowledge-in-pieces: wrong statements are local pieces, so a student can apply a piece at one point and not another.

L1.names_the_element.quote: is still learning to recognise syntax and distinguish between the various elements of code
L1.names_the_element.note: L0/L1 edge: recognising and distinguishing code elements is what the sensorimotor novice is still acquiring.

L1.names_the_element.quote: This is a response where the student manifests a correct grasp of some but not all aspects of the problem.
L1.names_the_element.note: SOLO unistructural: correct but partial grasp (one aspect).

L1.names_the_element.quote: When a student has a partial understanding, the student makes what the Leeds Working group called an "educated guess".
L1.names_the_element.note: Observable L1 behaviour on MCQs: educated guessing from partial understanding.

L1.names_the_element.quote: Unistructural Provides a description for one portion of the code (i.e. describes the if statement)
L1.names_the_element.note: Whalley table: unistructural = describes one portion of the given code (e.g. only the if statement).

L1.names_the_element.quote: Demonstrates some understanding of the code beyond the types of statements,
L1.names_the_element.note: Score 1: goes beyond naming statement types but stays low level; boundary with score 0 is 'beyond the types of statements'.

L1.names_the_element.quote: This is a response where the student manifests a correct grasp of some but not all aspects of the programming problem.
The response focuses on a single statement or concept

L1.states_the_rule.quote: novice programming students are likely t o vehemently deny that the computer can think or that it is intelligent
L1.states_the_rule.note: Stating the right rule (computer is mechanistic) does not prevent applying the wrong one: L1 statement can coexist with L0 behaviour.

L1.states_the_rule.quote: This is a response where the student manifests a correct grasp of some but not all aspects of the problem.
L1.states_the_rule.note: Same unistructural definition applies to stating one correct rule without integrating the rest.

L1.states_the_rule.quote: These skills span from understanding syntax (as the easiest), to code tracing (executing code in your head for one particular input), to code reading/explaining (abstracting the behavior of code across all inputs), to code writing (as the most complex) [11].
L1.states_the_rule.note: Hierarchy places syntax knowledge below tracing: knowing the rule (L1) < applying it to one input (L2) < across all inputs (L3) < writing (L4).

L1.states_the_rule.quote: while a student may be able to articulate particular items of knowledge when explicitly prompted for any of them, when that student is asked to apply that knowledge in a program writing context, the student “sort of knows, has some fragments, can make some moves, has a notion, without being able to marshal enough knowledge with sufficient precision to carry a problem through to a clean solution”
L1.states_the_rule.note: 'Fragile knowledge': stating a rule when prompted (L1) is separable from applying it to code (L2+); an answer that only articulates the rule stays L1.

L1.states_the_rule.quote: Code reiteration/plagiarism from other programming tasks or educational material
L1.states_the_rule.note: Table 1 unistructural: reproducing a taught pattern without applying it is L1.

L1.states_the_rule.quote: They advocated that students' answers should be categorized in the unistructural level of the SOLO taxonomy when a specific problem or programming situation has been encountered in the class.
L1.states_the_rule.note: Petersen et al. cited: reproducing a problem seen in class is L1, so level depends on what was taught.

L1.states_the_rule.quote: In many cases, students make what is called an "educated guess" (Lister et al., 2004).
L1.states_the_rule.note: Unistructural answers are often guesses from one cue.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: Preoperational students can trace code. That is, they can manually execute a piece of code and determine the values in the variables when the execution is finished.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Defines the preoperational trace.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: The novice can reliably manually execute ("trace") multiple lines of code.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Tracing stage = reliable multi-line trace.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: A lineíbyíline description is a SOLO multistructural response, while a correct summary of the overall computation is a SOLO relational response.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: L2/L3 edge in EPE coding: line-by-line = multistructural; summary = relational.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: A defining characteristic of preoperational reasoning in programming is that, while such a novice can reliably trace code, that novice does not routinely abstract from the code to see a meaningful computation performed by that code.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Upper edge of L2: reliable trace without abstracted purpose.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: However, the preoperational novice is heavily reliant on the use of specific values to trace, understand and write code.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Hallmark: tracing with specific values.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: Preoperational novices are preoccupied with the detail of a tracing task.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Detail-bound trace; effort hides purpose ('tracing blind').

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: For the novice who is thinking preoperationally, the lines in a piece of code are only weakly related.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Lines traced as weakly related units.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: This is a response where the student manifests an understanding of all parts of the problem, but does not manifest an awareness of the relationships between these parts - the student fails to see the forest for the trees.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: SOLO multistructural: all parts, no relations.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: Multistructural A line by line description is provided of all the code. Summarization of individual statements may be included
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Whalley table: multistructural = line-by-line description of all the code.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: For someone who does not seek to abstract, the focus of attention is on the individual lines of code as separate entities, not on the relationships between those lines of code.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: L2 focus: lines as separate entities.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: but is far from constructing a high-level description. Either uses a very low level
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Score 1 band: very low abstraction (line-by-line) or several errors.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: Central to this is the ability to distinguish between two response types: multi-structural, where students describe the code line-by-line, and relational, where they explain the code's overall purpose.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Smith's operational split L2 vs L3.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: Using a Large Language Model (LLM) to segment both the student's description and the code, we aim to determine whether the student describes each line individually (many segments) or the code as a whole (fewer segments).
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Boundary L2/L3 as segment count: many segments mapped to separate lines = L2.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: Responses containing a number of segments above each of given thresholds is classified as multistructural and those at or below are classified as relational.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Threshold rule: segments > t -> multistructural; <= t -> relational.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: The model achieved its highest performance at a threshold of 2, with 81% agreement, a Cohen's 𝜅 of 0.61, an F1 score of 0.80, precision of 0.83, and recall of 0.81.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Best raw threshold: more than 2 segments = multistructural.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: To address this, we implemented a post-processing step that removed segments containing only function definitions.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: After dropping signature-only segments, thresholds 1 and 2 perform about equally (kappa 0.61).

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: For example, a multi-structural response might describe the behavior of individual parts of the code without identifying their collective purpose, yet would be graded by CGBG as equally correct compared to a relational response that does describe the abstract goal.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Multistructural can be functionally correct; correctness and level are separate dimensions.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: Beginning with questions A-Q1 and B-Q4, the researchers classified the responses as either multistructural correct, relational correct, or incorrect.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Human coding scheme: three classes; correctness is crossed with level only for correct answers.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: In particular, programmers need to be able to understand code at the relational level (i.e., can summarize the code's purpose) and not just the multistructural (i.e., line-by-line) level [39].
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Fowler's gloss of the two levels.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: We found that students were otherwise prone to give long, low-level, and over-complete answers, which are both more time consuming to score and often don't demonstrate whether the student is capable of a brief, high-level description.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Unprompted students default to L2; long over-complete answers do not show L3 capability.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: we use the term “fragile knowledge” to also include basic skills, such as the ability to systematically, manually execute (“trace”) a piece of code.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Defines tracing as systematic manual execution of code - the L2 line-by-line way.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: We use this term to describe any transcript for a question where the student hand executes the code in meticulous detail.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: 'Walkthrough' = think-aloud evidence of a line-by-line trace; coding rule for L2 trace in transcripts.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: They note that, while close tracking is an important skills for diagnosing bugs, it is mentally demanding, and therefore many students do not track their code carefully.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Perkins' 'close tracking' = line-by-line trace; cognitively demanding, so often skipped.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: If a student employs a thorough walkthrough to find the answer, it cannot be inferred that the student did not make any higher-level inference about the code.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Caution for coding: presence of a trace does not prove absence of L3 reasoning; level must be read from what is stated.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: The principal difference between top quartile students and the other two quartiles is that the top quartile students were more meticulous in the walkthrough process, and therefore made fewer errors.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Quality of L2 tracing = meticulousness; weaker students use the same method with more slips.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: Not surprisingly, Table 4.2 indicates that, if a student carefully traces through the code (S, T, or O), thus documenting changes in variables, the likelihood of getting the correct answer is high. In contrast, not doodling (B) only leads to the correct answer 50% of the time.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Table 4.2: S 77%, T 75%, O 78% correct vs B (blank) 50%; documenting variable changes separates a real trace from a guess.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: The student focuses on several relevant aspects but does not manifest an awareness of the relationships between them or the whole.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: SOLO multistructural definition.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: However, he is not able to see the code as a single coherent construct.
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: L2 vs L3: no view of the code as one construct.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: The response describes the largest part of the code (line by line) without focusing on the relations among parts/statements
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Table 1 multistructural.

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: The response describes the largest part of the code (line by line) with minor flaws in the description
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Minor flaws allowed at L2; covering most of the code separates L2 from L1 (one part).

L2.line_by_line_trace.quote: The response just describes one part of the code
L2.line_by_line_trace.note: Table 1 unistructural: one part only, the L1 side of the boundary.

L2.output_prediction.quote: It is the process that identifies concrete operational reasoning, not the final answer.
L2.output_prediction.note: Supports requiring a value-by-value justification: the answer alone does not fix the level.

L2.output_prediction.quote: With multiple choice questions, it is not possible to assign a student's response to a SOLO level when only provided with the option chosen by the student. Knowledge is required of how the student chose that option.
L2.output_prediction.note: Supports the graph's requirement that output_prediction carry a value-by-value justification: the chosen value alone cannot be levelled.

L2.output_prediction.quote: These skills span from understanding syntax (as the easiest), to code tracing (executing code in your head for one particular input), to code reading/explaining (abstracting the behavior of code across all inputs), to code writing (as the most complex) [17].
L2.output_prediction.note: Output prediction = one input (L2); purpose = all inputs (L3).

L2.output_prediction.quote: For example, if a student chooses an answer, without a complete walkthrough, then either the student has made a guess, or the student has employed some sort of higher-level reasoning strategy.
L2.output_prediction.note: A bare correct output is ambiguous (guess or L3); supports requiring a value-by-value justification for L2 output_prediction.

L2.output_prediction.quote: 3) The student is either guessing, or has heuristics for selecting a plausible answer without genuinely understanding the MCQ, which is essentially an educated guess.
L2.output_prediction.note: One reading of a blank-page (no-trace) correct MCQ answer: guessing/heuristics, not L2.

L2.output_prediction.quote: if a student got a skill correct then they most definitely have mastered that skill because guessing the correct answer on open-ended questions is near impossible.
L2.output_prediction.note: Open-ended output answers resist guessing (unlike MCQ); contrast with Lister's MCQ guessing caveat.

L2.one_step_execution.quote: Preoperational novices are not yet able to perform abstract reasoning about a chunk of code, as their focus is quite narrow: limited to simply a single statement or expression at a time.
L2.one_step_execution.note: Unit of preoperational reasoning is one statement or expression.

L2.one_step_execution.quote: They have developed the ability to determine the functional outcome of each line of code and trace to completion.
Also, the thinking tends to focus on only one abstract property at any given moment in time

Unlike tracing, which focuses on predicting the behavior of individual lines, EiPE tasks require students to articulate the purpose of code segments in natural language, emphasizing abstract reasoning [19].
L2.one_step_execution.note: Predicting the behaviour of individual lines (tracing) is below EiPE purpose statements.

L2.one_step_execution.quote: For example, the student describes the functioning of a part (one or two lines) of the code.
L2.one_step_execution.note: The paper uses describing one or two lines as its UNISTRUCTURAL example; see placement_flags.

L3.relation_to_neighbour.quote: They struggle to recognise the relationship between two or more statements.
L3.relation_to_neighbour.note: L2/L3 edge: relating two or more statements is beyond the preoperational novice.

L3.relation_to_neighbour.quote: concrete operational novice is the ability to perform transitive inference: comparing two objects via an intermediary object.
L3.relation_to_neighbour.note: Transitive inference = relating two constructs via a third.

L3.relation_to_neighbour.quote: Their thinking reflects the direct manipulations they could make to that environment. There is little thinking about the relationships between the objects.
From the neo-Piagetian perspective, the reason why a novice may not be able to perform transitive inference is that the working memory of the novice is overloaded by other information
L3.relation_to_neighbour.note: Why relating fails at L2: working memory, not missing rule knowledge.

L3.relation_to_neighbour.quote: Transitive inference is a defining quality of the concrete operational stage.
L3.relation_to_neighbour.note: Anchors transitive inference at concrete operational.

L3.relation_to_neighbour.quote: Often, utterances like the above occur after a detailed examination of the loop, or after hand executing one or two iterations.
L3.relation_to_neighbour.note: Partial abstractions often follow a short trace (L2 -> L3 path).

L3.relation_to_neighbour.quote: One important difference from novice programmers is that experts can automatically 'chunk' multiple syntax elements and process them as one unit [6, 12, 15, 25, 41], which reduces their cognitive load [35].
L3.relation_to_neighbour.note: Chunking several constructs into one unit = relation between neighbouring constructs.

L3.relation_to_neighbour.quote: The student makes sense of the various aspects of the topic, integrates the parts of the problem into a coherent code structure, and uses this structure to solve the problem.
The response shows integration of programming concepts and constructs
A relational response is the most sophisticated type of response a student may give and may be either correct or incorrect.
L3.relation_to_neighbour.note: Relational can be incorrect; see placement_flags.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: By the time a novice is at the concrete operational stage, their focus shifts from individual statements to small chunks of code which allows them to consider the overall purpose of code.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Defines purpose reasoning on chunks.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: These novice programmers reason about code deductively, by reading the code itself, rather than using the preoperational inductive approach.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Deductive (L3) vs inductive (L2) route to purpose.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: the novice who is thinking preoperationally may make a reasonable inductive guess, based upon the input/output behaviour they observe from tracing the code, but that novice will not infer the computation deductively, from the code itself.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Edge: a purpose obtained by induction from I/O pairs is L2; deduced from code is L3.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: As novices at the preoperational stage attempt to reason about code, they tend to make guesses based on intuition, and those intuitions can be inconsistent.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: L2 descriptor for failed purpose attempts.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: He was reasoning about the parts of the code as he read and traced the code.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Process marker of concrete reasoning.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: This is a response where the student integrates the parts of the problem into a coherent structure, and uses that structure to solve the task - the student sees the forest.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: SOLO relational definition.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Relational Provides a summary of what the code does in terms of the code's purpose.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Whalley table: relational = summary in terms of purpose.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: In fact, many students did supply both, and those students were categorized as having provided a relational response.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: An answer with both line-by-line and purpose is coded at the higher (relational) level.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: For someone who actively seeks to abstract from concrete code, it is natural to provide a relational response to the instruction "explain in plain English".
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: L3 behaviour: abstracts from concrete code unprompted.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: In providing such a response, a student manifests an ability to read several lines of code and integrate them into a coherent structure - to see the forest, not just the trees.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Relational = integration of several lines into one structure.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Clearly and correctly articulates all of the key ideas at a suitably high level of
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Score 6 begins: all key ideas, high level, nothing wrong.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: descriptions, as long as they are consistent with the code.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Score 6 may contain line-level detail if consistent - matches Lister's 'both' rule.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Articulates key ideas at a high level of abstraction, but contains improper or
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Score 5: high level, improper English/syntax but no wrong programming interpretation.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Articulates key ideas, but an incorrect interpretation is possible due to imprecise use of language or an insufficiently high level of abstraction.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Score 4: likely understood, but ambiguous or not abstract enough.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: A notable example in this category is explicitly saying that the code modifies a local variable without indicating that the local variable is returned.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Score 4 marker: purpose stated in terms of a local variable not the return value.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Does not contain enough information to be clearly categorized as absolutely right
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Score 3: under-specified, nothing clearly wrong.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: If aspects of an answer potentially fit multiple categories, we assigned the answer to the lowest category.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Global tie-break: lowest category.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: In mapping the three-dimensional space of (level of abstraction, correctness, ambiguity) to a linear scale we (in hindsight) most valued answers that were correct and at a high level of abstraction, but we were more tolerant of ambiguity.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Rubric weights: abstraction and correctness over ambiguity.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: We found that the source of our scoring difficulty arose from the fact that student answers varied importantly in three dimensions: level of abstraction (as per the SOLO-inspired scale), correctness, and ambiguity.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Three dimensions; SOLO only covers abstraction.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Our binary scores corresponded to 0-4 (incorrect) and 5-6 (correct) on a previously validated scoring rubric [4].
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Binary cut on Chen scale: 5-6 = correct relational.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Correct responses must be correct at the relational level (non line-by-line descriptions) and unambiguous.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Correct = relational + correct + unambiguous.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Extra information or word order leading to an incorrect meaning tend to be ignored.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Keyword graders miss relational errors carried by extra information/word order - a human must check correctness of the whole.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: As seen from our results, particularly after some degree of post-processing has occurred, guiding students towards responses that contain 1-2 segments is likely to coincide with guiding them away from multi-structural responses and towards relational ones.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: 1-2 segments ~ relational.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: The number of purple blocks indicates how many segments were parsed and thus how close an answer is to being relational, with an ideal relational answer having a single segment (one purple block) that represents the entire function.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Ideal L3 = one segment covering entire function.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Tracing provides an important foundation, enabling students to understand program flow by simulating execution step-by-step, and explaining builds on this by requiring students to abstract and articulate the purpose of code, moving from a line-by-line analysis to a broader conceptual understanding.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Explaining (L3) builds on tracing (L2).

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: However, it is worth noting that the standard deviations for the segmentation counts is reasonably high, meaning there is a significant overlap between the distributions which places an upper limit on the degree to which said distributions can be separated.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Segment count is a noisy indicator; not a sufficient rule alone.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: a weakness of non-idiomatic code is that it encourages students to mechanically hand execute code, when we would also like them to read with the aim of abstracting to schema.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Tasks with non-idiomatic code elicit L2 tracing; idiomatic code is needed to elicit L3 abstraction.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: whether or not the answers reached the relational level of the SOLO
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: EiPE credit only if the answer is relational (SOLO) - the L2/L3 boundary used for grading.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: we were concerned that if students were instead required to explain the function of a piece of code, poor performance might be due to a lack of eloquence, not a lack of understanding of the code
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Explain tasks confound language with understanding - a caution when coding L3.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Most students performed excellently in four of the skills, with explaining code as the exception.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Explain is the hardest of five skills (mean 47%).

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: For example, a student is able to describe the function performed by a particular code segment without hand executing.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Purpose without tracing.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: The response shows understanding of the purpose and the functionality of the code
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Table 1 relational descriptor 1.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: The classification of each response was examining whether a student is able to identify the purpose of a code segment rather than focusing on the correctness of that code.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Purpose, not correctness, decides L3.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: As Lister et al. (2006) argued, the students who are not able to read and describe a programming code relationally do not possess the skills needed to autonomously create their own code to solve similar problems.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Relational reading is a prerequisite for writing.

L3.purpose_of_the_whole.quote: Research findings indicate that expert programmers form abstract representations based upon the purpose of the code whereas novices form concrete representations based on how the code functions.
L3.purpose_of_the_whole.note: Purpose vs function contrast behind L3 vs L2.

L4.predict_a_change.quote: The archetypal manifestation of concrete thinking is the ability to reason about quantities that are conserved, and processes that are reversible.
L4.predict_a_change.note: Defines reversibility and conservation as the core of concrete reasoning.

L4.predict_a_change.quote: Note, however, that we cannot conclude that a novice has performed concrete operational reasoning if the only evidence we have is the novice
L4.predict_a_change.note: Evidence condition: final code alone, produced on a computer, does not prove concrete reasoning.

L4.predict_a_change.quote: Younger children, who are thinking in a preoperational mode, will give different answers depending on the height of the water in the two glasses.
L4.predict_a_change.note: Preoperational failure on conservation: answer follows one surface measure.

L4.predict_a_change.quote: A child or adult who reasons concretely and correctly first begins to do so when an increase in working memory capacity due to chunking allows them to consider two measures of the quantity of liquid in a glass
L4.predict_a_change.note: Concrete edge: two measures held at once.

L4.predict_a_change.quote: we found that trace is a prerequisite to the explain, sequence, and write skills while a reverse trace is a prerequisite to explain.
L4.predict_a_change.note: Reverse trace precedes explain; trace -> reverse trace was not significant after Bonferroni.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: What Edwards was describing is hypothetico-deductive reasoning, a signature skill of formal operational reasoning.
A programmer who is thinking in a formal operational manner routinely applies general debugging principles like these.
Consequently, the hypothetico-deductive reasoning of formal operational reasoning tends not to be manifested in concrete reasoning.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Concrete reasoners do not typically show hypothesis-driven diagnosis.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: When writing code, these novices tend to patch and repatch their
Errors are not always discovered, as the test cases on which the program is tested are very limited.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Ginat: limited testing; outside source points out falsifying input.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: A patch is offered. Sometimes the patch is sufficient for yielding correctness, but more often than not, the patch is insufficient.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Patching without generalising the failing input class.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: burrow right into the problem data as quickly as possible
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Concrete approach hugs the given data; speculations about other possibilities are a last resort.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: In this highest SOLO level, the student response goes beyond the immediate problem to be solved, and links the problem to a broader context.
Perkins et. al (1989) claim that the ability to perform a walkthrough is an important skill for diagnosing bugs, and therefore the ability to review code is an important skill in writing code.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Tracing is the tool for diagnosis.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: the ability to read what a piece of code actually does, rather than what we might think on a first quick inspection, is an important debugging skill.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Diagnosis rests on reading actual, not intended, behaviour (non-idiomatic Q2).

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: We use the term "error" to describe a concrete incidence of a student making a mistake while trying to understand a program, leading to wrong assumptions about how that program behaves.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: An error is the observable incident; diagnosing it means tracing it back to the difficulty behind it.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: Errors are therefore the materialization of difficulties.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Diagnose = going from the materialized error to the underlying difficulty/misconception.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: This is not the case, showing that the time to fix an error is not noticeably related to how often a student will encounter it.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Frequency and difficulty to diagnose are separate dimensions.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: Mistake severity is literally measured by the time spent fixing it.
educators may still be accurate about the cause of mistakes and student's conceptions of the mistakes, but just not about the frequency and time-to-fix of such mistakes.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Cause (the misconception behind) is what diagnosis targets, not frequency.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: Therefore, instructors might wish to focus on generic programming errors over specific programming errors when providing interventions to help students.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Diagnose to the generic (conceptual) class, not the surface instance.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: A frequent error is not necessarily problematic if easily detected and fixed by students, and in fact some would argue that such detecting/fixing is an important part of the learning process.
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Easily fixed errors are not strong evidence for L4.

L4.diagnose_an_error.quote: Misconceptions include a description of the symptoms one can expect students holding that misconception to exhibit (e.g., code smells or erroneous snippets of code observed in students' solutions, which can point to the misconception).
L4.diagnose_an_error.note: Symptoms are what a diagnosis starts from; diagnosis goes from symptom to misconception.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: This stage is the first stage where students begin to show a purposeful approach to writing code.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Concrete operational = purposeful writing.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: These novices struggle to truly design a solution.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Preoperational writers cannot design.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: When they do produce a "clean compile" the code may bear little resemblance to the problem to be solved, and the code may even contain aspects that are bizarre to an experienced programmer.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Sensorimotor writing.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Such students can only write code by quasi-random mutation.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Preoperational writing.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Some other students tend to reason in a concrete operational form, where they can see some abstractions of specific code, but they can only see those abstractions in the context of that specific code.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Concrete abstractions tied to the given code; transfer beyond it is not concrete.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: If they cannot reason about code given to them, then they are probably incapable of writing similar code.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Reading/explaining precedes writing similar code.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Formal operational thinking can involve reasoning about hypothetical situations, or at least reasoning about situations that have never been directly experienced by the thinker.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Novel/hypothetical situations = formal operational.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: In our view, students who cannot read a short piece of code and describe it in relational terms are not intellectually well equipped to write similar code.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: L3 reading is a prerequisite for writing similar code (transfer).

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: We believe that if a student is to be adept at writing code, and debugging that code, then the relational response needs to become the natural and most obvious way of explaining what code does - just as the relational response appears to be the natural and obvious mode of explanation for seven of the eight educators.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Writing and debugging rest on relational reading.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: For code writing questions, the correlation is 0.555, which is significantly positive (p < 0.0001).
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: EiPE score correlates with writing at r=0.555.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Their weakness is the inability to reliably work their way through the long chain of reasoning required to hand execute code, and/or an inability to reason reliably at a more abstract level to select the missing line of code.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Separates the L2 failure (hand execution) from the higher-level failure (selecting missing code).

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Our findings matched the previous finding that tracing is a prerequisite for students to learn to write code.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Supports placing writing (L4 transfer) above tracing (L2).

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Our findings show that for both thresholds, tracing is a prerequisite skill before learning how to write, explain, and sequence code.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Tracing is the base skill for every other skill.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Contradicting the previous claims, our analysis showed that using the mean threshold writing code is a prerequisite to explaining code. However, there is no clear relationship when we change the threshold to the median.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Writing (L4) may precede explaining (L3) - see placement flag.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: This suggests that as students improve their overall programming ability, code writing ability and explaining ability tend to grow in tandem
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Write and explain co-develop at higher ability.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: We accept that a student who scores well on the type of tests used in this study, but who cannot write novel code of similar complexity, is most likely suffering from a weakness in problem solving.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Reading/tracing success is necessary but not sufficient for writing new code.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Furthermore, the authors of this paper believe that it may be appropriate to first teach systematic tracing as a base skill, then allow students to build these higher-level comprehension skills upon that base.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Ordering: tracing (L2) before higher-level comprehension (L3/L4).

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: the largest finding of their work was that tracing may be a prerequisite for reading code, which may then be a prerequisite for writing code.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Lopez et al. 2008 hierarchy trace -> explain -> write, as summarised by Pradhan Newar.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Yamamoto, Sekiya, and Yamaguchi (2011) replicated the work of Lopez et al. (2008) using the Structural equation model and found that students ability to edit existing code and write new code from scratch depends on their ability to explain code.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Prior evidence that explain (L3) underlies edit and write (L4).

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: In this highest SOLO level, the student response goes beyond the particular problem to be solved, and links the problem to a broader context.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: SOLO extended abstract definition.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: The student is able to extrapolate, to develop higher order principles and extend the topic to wider application areas.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: EA behaviours.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Questioning and going beyond key programming principles or the problem assigned
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Table 1 EA descriptor 1.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: The response relates a programming concept or principle in a way that indicates students' ability to handle new or unseen problems
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Table 1 EA descriptor 2.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Ideally, the classification of responses into the level of extended abstract indicates students' ability a) to use programming principles and constructs that were not explicitly taught and/or b) to move beyond the problem assigned.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: EA needs untaught constructs or going past the problem.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: On the top of the proposed hierarchy is students' ability to write, correct and improve non-trivial code segments with the aim to solve a specific problem.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: Lister et al. 2009 hierarchy cited: writing, correcting and improving is the top level.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: While this is a very interesting level to study, the tasks designed for the present study do not aimed at promoting students' performance in the extended abstract level.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: No EA data in the variable/assignment study.

L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.quote: Therefore, the tasks included in the present study were not expected to record students' performance in the extended abstract level.
L4.transfer_to_a_new_program.note: No EA data in the arrays study.

L0.name: Prestructural / sensorimotor
L0.criterion_template: An answer is at L0 for {c} when it shows no working model of {c}: it reads the code with everyday or maths meanings, applies a documented wrong rule, or traces it accurately only now and then.
L0.deciding_question_template: Does every rule the answer applies to {c} agree with the language rule? If it reads the code with everyday meanings, applies a wrong rule, or switches rules within one trace, it is L0. A slip in an otherwise rule-correct trace is L2 with an error, not L0.

L1.name: Unistructural / atom x text surface
L1.criterion_template: An answer is at L1 for {c} when it grasps one correct aspect of {c}: it names or describes one part of the given code, or states the rule of {c}, without covering all parts or applying the rule to the values.
L1.deciding_question_template: Does the answer cover every part of the code, in order, with the values (L2)? If it covers one part or only states the rule, it is L1.

L2.name: Multistructural / block x execution / preoperational
L2.criterion_template: An answer is at L2 for {c} when it covers all parts of the code that use {c}, line by line or value by value, without relating them to what the code is for. It may be correct, or a multistructural error.
L2.deciding_question_template: Is the answer many segments mapped onto lines (L2), or one segment stating the purpose of the whole (L3)? A correct output with no value-by-value justification is not levelled.

L3.name: Relational / relations x function (concrete operational begins)
L3.criterion_template: An answer is at L3 for {c} when it integrates the parts into one structure: it relates {c} to another construct in the same code, or states in one sentence what the code does, deduced from the code. It may be correct, or a relational error.
L3.deciding_question_template: Was the purpose deduced from the code, or only guessed from traced input/output pairs (then L2)? Does the answer stay within the given code (L3), or reason about changed code, an error class or a new program (L4)?

L4.name: Extended abstract (concrete-operational reversibility and conservation)
L4.criterion_template: An answer is at L4 for {c} when it goes beyond the given code with the rule of {c}: it predicts a change by reasoning about what is conserved, states the class of inputs under which an error shows, or solves an unseen problem.
L4.deciding_question_template: Does the answer link the code to a broader context: a changed program, a class of inputs, an unseen problem? Re-tracing changed code value by value is L2; fixing one given failing case is L3.

ways.rule_template: The answer reads {c} with natural-language, everyday or maths meanings (for example treating = as equality, or the program as a mind that grasps intent) instead of {rule}, so it states nothing that agrees with that rule. A word-for-word English transliteration of the statements also stays here.
ways.boundary_template: Any correct, programming-specific statement about {c} makes the answer L1 or higher.

ways.rule_template: The answer applies, consistently, the documented wrong rule "{wrong}", a statement the language rule disproves: {right}
ways.boundary_template: A single slip in an otherwise rule-correct trace is L2 with an error. Style or strategy breaches are not language misconceptions, and beliefs about a library are tagged scope=library.
ways.literature_disagreement: Jimoyiannis 2011 codes some answers driven by a misconception as unistructural or multistructural, not prestructural.

ways.rule_template: Within one trace of code using {c}, the answer applies the correct rule at one occurrence and the contradicting rule "{wrong}" at another, so it follows no single model and is only occasionally accurate.
ways.boundary_template: A bookkeeping slip under one consistent, correct rule is L2 with an error, not L0.
ways.literature_disagreement: Lister 2006 codes by technique: an error inside a systematic hand trace is still multistructural.

ways.rule_template: The answer correctly names or describes one part of the given code that is {c} ({desc}), without covering the other parts or how they relate.
ways.boundary_template: Covering every part of the code in order is L2.

ways.rule_template: The answer states {rule}, or recites a taught example of it, but does not apply it to the values of the given code (fragile knowledge).
ways.boundary_template: Applying the rule to this code's values is L2. Stating a rule that the language disproves is L0.

ways.rule_template: The answer hand-executes or describes each statement of the code that uses {c}, in execution order and with the specific values, following {rule}, and interprets what each statement does, without stating what the whole computes.
ways.boundary_template: One segment stating the purpose of the whole is L3. A word-for-word transliteration with no interpretation is L0 (Chen score 0).

ways.rule_template: The answer gives the output or final values of the code that uses {c} and justifies them value by value through the execution.
ways.boundary_template: A bare correct output is not levelled: it may be a guess, or hide a misconception. A prediction justified by the code's purpose is L3.
ways.literature_disagreement: Jimoyiannis 2011 codes a correct output justified with a value table as relational.

ways.rule_template: The answer gives the correct state change produced by one execution of {c}, e.g. one value after one statement or one condition evaluated with given values.
ways.boundary_template: This counts as L2 only when that single step is the whole fragment asked about. Describing one or two lines of a longer fragment is L1.

ways.rule_template: In code that contains both {c} and {n}, the answer relates them, explaining how the effect of one depends on the other ({link}), and uses that relation to explain the code.
ways.boundary_template: Two correct but separate rules are L1. Executing the two in sequence is L2. A relational answer may be correct or a relational error.

ways.rule_template: The answer states in one sentence what code that uses {c} does for all inputs, deduced from the code and not guessed from traced input/output pairs. It is correct when all key ideas are stated unambiguously (Chen 5-6).
ways.boundary_template: Narrating the lines is L2. A purpose induced from a few traced cases is L2. A wrong purpose is still L3, but with an error.

ways.rule_template: Given a small change to {c} in the code{mc}, the answer predicts the new behaviour by reasoning from what the code achieves and what the change conserves or reverses, without re-tracing from scratch.
ways.boundary_template: Re-tracing the changed code value by value is L2 on the new code. Adapting given code to a familiar variant may be only relational.
ways.literature_disagreement: Jimoyiannis 2011 and Vrachnos & Jimoyiannis 2017 code modification of given code as relational, not extended abstract.

ways.rule_template: For code with the mistake "{wrong}", the answer locates it, names the rule it breaks ({right}), and states the general class of inputs or conditions under which it shows, so that the fix holds for all inputs.

LT.rule: The same order as any loop: test, body, test... In an infinite loop the update either never runs or never moves the tested variables towards false, so every test yields true.

sources.quote: Second, nothing might happen. If your program has an infinite loop that does not produce any output, it will spin through the loop and you will see no results at all.

concepts.label: Reasoning about loops
concepts.description: convincing yourself a loop is correct by stating facts that hold each time through it and why it terminates

rules.quote: Reasoning of this sort is often important in understanding how while loops work.

concepts.note: Added in v3.2 from the book-to-graph coverage check; the books name no misconception for it.

E.rule: Folk meaning: in everyday life 'convincing yourself' means trying a few cases, so a novice thinks a loop is correct because it worked on the inputs tried. Loop reasoning requires a fact that holds before every test, a reason it survives each pass, and a reason the loop ends, so the argument covers any number of iterations.

sources.quote: Reasoning of this sort is often important in understanding how while loops work.
The logic behind such arguments is the same whether the loop iterates just a few times, as in TenHellos, dozens of times, as in PowersOfTwo, or millions of times

S.rule: For `int v = 1; while (v <= N/2) v = 2*v;`: (1) v is always a power of 2; (2) v is never greater than N; (3) v increases each pass, so the loop terminates; (4) after the loop, 2*v > N. So v is the largest power of 2 that is ≤ N.

sources.quote: v is always a power of 2.
v is never greater than N.
v increases each time through the loop, so the loop must terminate.

sources.quote: Reasoning of this sort is often important in understanding how while loops work.

sources.quote: After the loop terminates, 2*v is greater than N.

sources.quote: v is always a power of 2.

E.rule: Folk meaning: everyday digits are decimal, so '10011' reads as ten thousand and eleven, and 'converting' sounds like changing the number. Binary conversion changes only the representation: 19 and 10011 (base 2) are the same integer, printed as a sequence of bits by casting out powers of 2.

sources.quote: Thinking about conversion emphasizes the distinction between an abstraction (an integer like the number of hours in a day) and a representation of that abstraction (24 or 11000).

S.rule: First find v, the largest power of 2 ≤ N (`while (v <= N/2) v = 2*v;`). Then, with n = N, for each v from there down to 1: if n < v print 0, else print 1 and set n -= v; then v = v/2.

if (n < v) { System.out.print(0); } else { System.out.print(1); n -= v; } v = v/2;

LT.rule: Order inside each pass: test `v > 0`; compare n < v; print the bit; subtract v from n only when the bit is 1; then halve v. The first loop runs to completion before the second begins.

P.rule: Plan: representation conversion. v is a stepper (powers of 2 in decreasing order), and n is the remaining excess that shrinks to 0. The same plan gives base-k conversion, and the right-to-left variant builds the string with `s = (n % 2) + s`.

sources.quote: A data item stepping through a systematic, predictable succession of values

concepts.label: Loop performance
concepts.description: the running time of a loop program depends on how many iterations it makes

rules.quote: Loops give us the ability to solve difficult problems, but they also give us the ability to construct simple programs that run slowly

concepts.note: Added in v3.2 from the book-to-graph coverage check; the books name no misconception for it.

E.rule: Folk meaning: 'computers are so fast it doesn't matter how many steps', so any correct loop is good enough. In fact running time grows with the number of iterations: an n-step loop over 10^18 values never finishes, while a √n-step loop finishes in seconds.

sources.quote: Even given the blinding speed of modern computers, such a decision would have a dramatic effect on the size of the numbers that we could factor.
Loops give us the ability to solve difficult problems, but they also give us the ability to construct simple programs that run slowly, so we must always be cognizant of performance.

T.rule: Applies the iteration-counting rule unevenly: one loop's passes are counted while an inner loop's passes are left out, or the loop is assumed to run N times when its condition (i <= n/i) stops it near √n, so the cost estimate is off by orders of magnitude.

sources.quote: The inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.
A student may make an error while hand executing the code, never-the-less the technique is multistructural.

N.rule: Performance concept: the running time of a loop program is roughly (number of iterations) × (cost per iteration), and the loop condition determines the number of iterations.

sources.quote: Loops give us the ability to solve difficult problems, but they also give us the ability to construct simple programs that run slowly, so we must always be cognizant of performance.
The running time of this program is proportional to T times the average number of bets.

S.rule: Running time is proportional to the total number of times the innermost statements execute. Nested loops multiply their counts, so Gambler takes T × (average bets), and changing a bound from n to √n changes the feasible input from about 10^9 to about 10^18.

sources.quote: The running time of this program is proportional to T times the average number of bets.
with the (i <= n/i) test we can factor numbers on the order of 1018 in a comparable amount of time.

LT.rule: Order of the estimate: count the passes of the outer loop; for each, count the passes of the inner loop; multiply (or sum); multiply by the cost of one pass of the innermost body.

sources.quote: The running time of this program is proportional to T times the average number of bets.

OP.rule: The result is an iteration count or time estimate. `for (i = 2; i <= n/i; i++)` runs about √n times, against about n times for `i < n`. Gambler 500 2500 100 makes about 100 × 10^6 bets (nearly 100 million random numbers).

sources.quote: For example, the third command below causes nearly 100 million random numbers to be generated.
with the (i <= n/i) test we can factor numbers on the order of 1018 in a comparable amount of time.

OS.rule: Each extra pass adds a constant amount of work. Adding 1 to the bound of a single loop adds one pass, while adding 1 to the bound of an outer loop adds a full run of the inner loop.

sources.quote: The inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

R.rule: The loop's condition and update set the iteration count. A tighter test that keeps correctness (i <= n/i instead of i < n) or a faster update (doubling instead of incrementing) can make the program dramatically faster with identical output.

sources.quote: In a more naïve implementation, we might simply have used the condition (i < n) to terminate the for loop.
with the (i <= n/i) test we can factor numbers on the order of 1018 in a comparable amount of time.

P.rule: Purpose: to predict whether a program will finish in reasonable time for its inputs, and to choose among correct loop formulations (bounds, nesting, reuse of previous results).

sources.quote: Loops give us the ability to solve difficult problems, but they also give us the ability to construct simple programs that run slowly, so we must always be cognizant of performance.
You will learn to be aware of and to estimate the running time of your programs.

Instead, we can make use of the term that was added in on the previous loop iteration and solve the problem with a single for loop

D.rule_broken: Iteration count must be kept feasible for the input size.
D.trigger: A naive bound (`i < n` when factoring an 18-digit number, or counting primes up to 10 million by trial division): the program appears to hang.

sources.quote: Note : if you are not careful, your program may not finish in a reasonable amount of time!
You might not know (or it might not matter) whether a loop is infinite or just very long.

D.trigger: Recomputing each Taylor term from scratch in a nested loop: correct output but needlessly slow.

sources.quote: This code is effective, but it is inefficient because the inner for loop recomputes all the values it computed on the previous iteration of the outer for loop.

concepts.label: Space-time tradeoff

concepts.origin: v3.9 external coverage audit: Primitive vs reference variables, memory diagrams: Think Java 9.1, Goldman et al. 2008 (PVR, MMR), MIT 6.092

learning_levels.name: Prestructural / sensorimotor
learning_levels.criterion: L0 for program text: the answer holds a rule that contradicts Java.
learning_levels.criterion_general: An answer is at L0 for program text when it shows no working model of program text: it reads the code with everyday or maths meanings, applies a documented wrong rule, or traces it accurately only now and then.
learning_levels.deciding_question: Does every rule the answer applies to program text agree with the language rule? If it reads the code with everyday meanings, applies a wrong rule, or switches rules within one trace, it is L0. A slip in an otherwise rule-correct trace is L2 with an error, not L0.

learning_levels.name: Unistructural / atom x text surface
learning_levels.criterion: L1 for program text: the answer states one correct rule without applying it.
learning_levels.criterion_general: An answer is at L1 for program text when it grasps one correct aspect of program text: it names or describes one part of the given code, or states the rule of program text, without covering all parts or applying the rule to the values.
learning_levels.deciding_question: Does the answer cover every part of the code, in order, with the values (L2)? If it covers one part or only states the rule, it is L1.

learning_levels.name: Multistructural / block x execution / preoperational
learning_levels.criterion: L2 for program text: the answer applies these rules to every part of the code, in order.
learning_levels.criterion_general: An answer is at L2 for program text when it covers all parts of the code that use program text, line by line or value by value, without relating them to what the code is for. It may be correct, or a multistructural error.
learning_levels.deciding_question: Is the answer many segments mapped onto lines (L2), or one segment stating the purpose of the whole (L3)? A correct output with no value-by-value justification is not levelled.

learning_levels.name: Relational / relations x function (concrete operational begins)
learning_levels.criterion: L3 for program text: the answer relates the parts by these rules.
learning_levels.criterion_general: An answer is at L3 for program text when it integrates the parts into one structure: it relates program text to another construct in the same code, or states in one sentence what the code does, deduced from the code. It may be correct, or a relational error.
learning_levels.deciding_question: Was the purpose deduced from the code, or only guessed from traced input/output pairs (then L2)? Does the answer stay within the given code (L3), or reason about changed code, an error class or a new program (L4)?

learning_levels.name: Extended abstract (concrete-operational reversibility and conservation)
learning_levels.criterion: L4 for program text: the answer reasons beyond the given code by these rules.
learning_levels.criterion_general: An answer is at L4 for program text when it goes beyond the given code with the rule of program text: it predicts a change by reasoning about what is conserved, states the class of inputs under which an error shows, or solves an unseen problem.
learning_levels.deciding_question: Does the answer link the code to a broader context: a changed program, a class of inputs, an unseen problem? Re-tracing changed code value by value is L2; fixing one given failing case is L3.
