misconceptions_and_errors.label: AbsAlwaysNonNegative
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Math.abs always returns a non-negative number.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) returns Integer.MIN_VALUE, which is negative.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: SEI CERT Java coding rule.

book_support.quote: Q. What is the value of Math.abs(-2147483648)? A. -2147483648. This strange (but true) result is a typical example of the effects of integer overflow.

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: The misunderstood thing is Math.abs; SW explains it as integer overflow, so math_library first and overflow second.

final_check.note: SW p46 Q&A.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: AccumulatorDeclaredInLoop
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Declaring sum inside the loop body keeps a running total across passes.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The accumulator must be declared and initialised before the loop.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Book 1.3 exercise: 'The variable sum should be defined outside the loop.'

book_support.quote: Before the loop, we initialize total to 0. Each time through the loop, we update total by adding one element from the array.
Generally the scope of a variable is comprised of the statements that follow the declaration in the same block as the declaration.

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: TJ 7.5 (reduce/accumulator) states that the accumulator is initialised before the loop; SW scope rule explains why a body-local sum restarts. No explicit warning.

paper_support.quote: Loop construction incoherent with remainder of code.

final_check.note: TJ 136 before-the-loop initialization.

external_validation.name: Loop construction incoherent with remainder of code.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: AllDoublesToAvoidDivision
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Reges & Stepp Ch. 2, CPE 'Forgetting to Cast' (style).

book_support.quote: More generally, use integers for countable things and floating-point numbers for measurable things.
But if you need absolute precision, use integers instead.
Java performs floating-point division when one or more operands are double values

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: TJ Appendix D gives this right after the integer-division reminder.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule_previous: Use int for counts and cast where a fraction is needed; changing all types is poor style.

final_check.note: Second clause (make one operand double / cast) is not in the TJ quotes; add TJ p45 'Java performs floating-point division when one or more operands are double values.' (exact).

misconceptions_and_errors.label: AmplitudeIsPitch
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Making the sample values larger raises the pitch of the note.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The amplitude (y-value) corresponds to the volume; the frequency sets the pitch.

book_support.quote: The amplitude (y-value) of a sound corresponds to the volume.
When you double or halve the frequency, you move up or down one octave on the scale.
control the volume (multiply each sample value by the volume)

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: correct_rule matches SW wording exactly.

final_check.note: "frequency sets the pitch" follows from the octave/frequency passage.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: AnyFrequencyPlayable
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: A sine wave of any frequency, e.g. 30,000 Hz, plays correctly with StdAudio.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: With 44,100 samples per second the highest frequency that can be reproduced is the Nyquist frequency, 22,050 Hz.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3 from an explicit warning, Q&A answer or exercise in the book.

book_support.quote: Why do I hear weird results on standard audio when I try to sonify a sine wave with a frequency of 30,000 Hertz (or more)?
The Nyquist frequency, defined as one-half the sampling frequency, represents the highest frequency that can be reproduced.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: AnyValueInAnyVariable
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Book 1.2 Web Exercise 14 (int a = 27 * "three"); adjacent: mistakes I calTyp / Q rtnTyp.

book_support.quote: As a general rule, a variable has to have the same type as the value you assign to it. For example, you cannot store a string in minute or an integer in message.
A common source of confusion is that some strings look like integers, but they are not.
Each variable always stores one of the permissible data-type values.

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: TJ shows message = 123; as not legal and int x = 1.1; as a compiler error.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ArgsAlwaysPresent
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: args[0] can always be read.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: If you run the program without typing the command-line argument it expects, reading args[0] fails with java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: 0.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Book 1.2 Web Exercise 13: run LeapYear with no argument.

book_support.quote: Most likely, you forgot to include a command-line argument:
The JVM is complaining that you ran the program but did not type an argument as promised.

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: SW 1.1 Q&A (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: 0). The book does not mention args.length being 0.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule_previous: With no command-line argument, args.length is 0 and args[0] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

final_check.note: 'args.length is 0' is not in the p22 quotes; p22 shows 'java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: 0' (exact) which supports the exception part.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ArgsAreNumbers
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: command-line args arrive already typed, no parsing needed
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: args[0] is always a String, so Integer.parseInt(args[0]) is needed to get its number.

book_support.quote: It's not clear from the output, but the elements of args are strings.
you can use args[0] within your program's body to represent the string that you type on the command line when it is executed
We use the Java library methods Integer.parseInt() and Double.parseDouble() for this purpose.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ArgumentOrderInferred
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Java works out from the variable names which argument goes where, so Math.pow(n, 2) and Math.pow(2, n) mean the same.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Arguments are written in the order the method's signature lists them; for example, Math.pow(a, b) raises a to the bth power.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3.1 from the uploaded paper.

book_support.quote: its name followed by arguments of the specified type, enclosed in parentheses and separated by commas
double pow(double a, double b) raise a to the bth power

misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule_previous: Arguments are matched to parameters by position only; the first argument goes to the first parameter, whatever the names.

paper_support.quote: Assumption that programs could identify the context of how variables are used
paper_support.comment: Paper example passes (a, b) to a user-defined subHelper where (b, a) was meant (3 occurrences, 2.7%); here applied to library methods.

final_check.note: Quote only says arguments are in parentheses separated by commas; positional matching is not stated. Supporting quote: SW p39 'double pow(double a, double b) raise a to the bth power' (exact).

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ArithmeticInsteadOfBoolean

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ElsIf

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ElseAlwaysExecutes
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: The else branch of an if-else statement always executes.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The else branch runs only when the if condition is false.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ElseIfChainExitsEarly
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: An else-if chain can finish before it has tested all its conditions, even when no branch has run.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The conditions of an else-if chain are tested in order until one is true; only then, or after the last test (and the final else), does the chain end.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ElseIfOrderIgnored
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: The conditions of an else-if chain can be tested in any order (e.g. the matching or most specific one first).
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The conditions are tested top to bottom and the first true one wins, so their order changes the result when conditions overlap.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3.4 from the uploaded literature.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ElseMatchesIndentation

misconceptions_and_errors.label: EmptyInnerLoopSkipsRest

misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3.4 from the uploaded literature.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ErrorLineIsFaultLine
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: The line number in a javac error is always the line that has the mistake.

book_support.quote: Sometimes the compiler reports the place in the program where the error was detected, not where it actually occurred.

But the compiler may not be able to tell you exactly what mistake you made, so the error message may be hard to understand.

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: The current correct_rule example (a missing ; is noticed on the next line) contradicts TJ, which says that for a missing semicolon 'the location of the error is correct'; both books use a missing brace as the example (SW: a missing second '{' is reported as ';' expected on line 4).
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule_previous: The compiler may report the line after the fault, e.g. a missing ; is noticed on the next line.

final_check.note: 'missing closing brace reported at end of file' is not in the quotes; SW p21-22 gives the omitted-second-brace example (Bad.java:4/7/8).

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ExpressionOnLeftOfAssignment
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Writes a + b = c; or 7 = a; as if = were a math equation.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The left side of an assignment must be a single variable; only the right side can be an expression.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ExtremeStartsAtZero
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: The running maximum can always start at 0.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Start the running maximum at the most negative possible value (Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, or the smallest int), so that the first value read replaces it.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: FalseConditionEndsProgram
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: A false condition with no else ends the program.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: When an if condition is false and there is no else, execution continues with the statement after the if.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: FalseConditionRestartsProgram
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3.4 from the uploaded literature.

paper_support.quote: Thinking that control goes back to the beginning of the program when the condition is false.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: FalseLoopRepeatsNextCode
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3.4 from the uploaded literature.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: FewTrialsAreExact
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: A short simulation gives the exact page ranks.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: A simulation only estimates the page ranks: RandomSurfer needs 10^n moves to get answers precise to n decimal places and many more moves for those answers to become accurate (tens of thousands of moves for two accurate places, millions for three).
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Tversky & Kahneman 1971: people regard a small random sample 'as highly representative'.

book_support.quote: Accuracy can be elusive. It is a mistake to assume that a program produces accurate answers simply because it can print numbers to many decimal places of precision.
RandomSurfer needs 10n moves to get answers precise to n decimal places and many more moves for those answers to stabilize to an accurate value.
increasing the number of iterations gives increasingly accurate estimates of the probability that the surfer lands on each page

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: '10n' in the extracted text is 10^n. SW's sample output with T=100 (0.24 0.23 0.16 0.25 0.12) vs T=1000000 illustrates the point.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule_previous: Increasing the number of iterations gives increasingly accurate estimates of the probability.

final_check.note: Rule says 10^n moves give n correct places; SW says 10^n gives precision and "many more moves" are needed for accuracy.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: FieldWidthIsIntegerDigits
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: %2.4f prints two digits before the decimal point and four after.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The number before the point is the width of the whole field; %7.2f means 7 characters in total with 2 digits after the decimal point.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3 from an explicit warning, Q&A answer or exercise in the book.

book_support.quote: If I use the format %2.4f for a double value, I get two digits before the decimal point and four digits after, right?
No, that specifies just four digits after the decimal point. The first value is the width of the whole field.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: FirstArgIsArgsOne

misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Counting starts at 0: the first argument is args[0], the second args[1].

book_support.quote: Note that the count starts at 0, so you refer to the first argument as args[0], the second one as args[1], the third one as args[2], and so forth.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: FixEveryErrorMessage
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Each error message is a separate mistake that needs its own fix.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: One fault can produce several messages; fix the first and recompile.

If the compiler reports 100 error messages, that doesn't mean there are 100 errors in your program.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: FloatingPointIsExact
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Math.sqrt(2) * Math.sqrt(2) == 2 is true.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: A double is an approximation, so the product is close to 2 but not equal to 2.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Book 1.2 exercise: 'What is the value of (Math.sqrt(2) * Math.sqrt(2) == 2)?' CSAwesome 1.7.4; Liang Ch. 3 Common Error 5; Horstmann Common Error 3.2 (title).

book_support.quote: What is the value of (Math.sqrt(2) * Math.sqrt(2) == 2) ?
Novice programmers should avoid comparing two floating-point numbers for equality.
You should probably never use the == operator with doubles.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ForInitRepeats
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ForIsConditional
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: The body of a for statement executes at most once.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The body of a for statement runs once for every pass on which the condition is true, which can be many times.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ForLoopPartSkipped
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization).
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.

paper_support.quote: Skipping the update step of a loop. The student thinks that the update step of a loop can be omitted after an iteration finishes.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ForUpdateBeforeBody
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: IdentifierCaseInsensitive
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

book_support.quote: Identifiers are case-sensitive, so Ab, ab, and AB are all different names.
In the Hello World program, System has to begin with an uppercase letter; system and SYSTEM won't work.
Remember that uppercase letters are not the same as lowercase letters.

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: The current correct_rule speaks only of variable names, but the wrong belief is about a method name (Println). TJ Exercise 1.3 also asks to replace println with Println; TJ 2.1 adds 'There is no such type as Int or string.'
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule_previous: Variable names are case-sensitive.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: IdiomOverridesCode
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3.4 from the uploaded literature.

paper_support.quote: This evidence tends to support the idea that many students are influenced by standard idioms, such as looping through an array from position 0 to position length-1, but are not yet comfortable enough with those idioms to know when not to use them.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: IfConditionCheckedInHindsight
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Whether the branch runs is decided by the condition after the branch, or from the point inside the body where the condition becomes true.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The condition is tested once, before the branch; the whole branch runs if it was true at that moment and none of it runs otherwise.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3.4 from the uploaded literature.

paper_support.quote: Thinking that a condition can be evaluated after the corresponding branch of the selection statement is completed and that if the condition is true AFTER executing the corresponding branch, the branch is executed.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: IfConditionWatched
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever).
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Added in v3.4 from the uploaded literature.

paper_support.quote: Thinking the condition is constantly being checked parallel to the execution of the program. In this misconception an if -statement gets executed as soon as its condition becomes true.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: InnerCounterOverwritesOuter

misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: All input to a program is fixed before it starts running.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: InputReadOnceBeforeLoop
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Reading a value once before the loop is enough; the loop will process each new input value.

misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: If a loop condition is false at first but would become true later, the loop still runs (it repeats or skips until the condition is true, then runs until it is false).

misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: How many times a loop runs is decided by what the program is meant to do, so it may go on after its condition is false.

misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: LoopImpliedByOneTest
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: LoopOutputSameEachPass
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: A loop prints the same thing on every pass; the changing loop variable does not affect what the body does.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: LoopTerminatingCondition

misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same.

misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Start with a working program and make small changes, compiling and testing after each one, so an error is always in the last change.

book_support.quote: Start with a working program and make small, incremental changes. At any point, if there is an error, you will know where to look.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: WrongArgumentType
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Calls a method with arguments of the wrong type, e.g. Math.sqrt("2").
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Each argument must have the type the method's API lists.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Mistake I calTyp.

book_support.quote: For each method invocation, make sure that the arguments you provide are in the right order and have the right type
followed by arguments of the specified type, enclosed in parentheses and separated by commas.

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: TJ Appendix D checklist item 6. Note that int arguments are widened automatically (Math.sqrt(2) is fine); only incompatible types such as String fail.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: WrongIterationCount
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Updates the loop counter so that the loop runs the wrong number of times.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: The init, test and update together decide the number of passes; trace them to check the count.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Caceffo et al. JD.1 and JD.4.

book_support.quote: It is worthwhile to carefully examine the behavior of programs that use loops by studying a trace of the program.
Even though many of the loops you will write are much simpler than this one, you should be sure to convince yourself that each loop you write is going to behave as you expect.

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: SW recommends tracing loop variables to check the iteration count; no explicit warning about miscounting.

paper_support.quote: Wrong update of a loop counter, leading to an incorrect number of loop iterations.
paper_support.comment: Paper example: i = 1; instead of i += 1; inside a while loop.

paper_support.quote: Improper update of loop counter.
Loop iterates an incorrect number of times.

final_check.note: Quotes give tracing advice, consistent with the rule.

external_validation.name: Loop iterates an incorrect number of times.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: WrongOperatorOrder
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: G * m1 * m2 / r * r divides by r squared.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: * and / are applied left to right, so it divides by r and then multiplies by r; use / (r * r).
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Caceffo et al. JB.7 'The order of operands and operators is wrong' (4.5%); book 1.2 Exercise 7. Provenance check: matches Caceffo JB.7 (not ProgMiscon).

book_support.quote: A physics student gets unexpected results when using the code F = G * mass1 * mass2 / r * r;
That is not correct, because multiplication and division have the same precedence, and they are evaluated from left to right.

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: SW Exercise 1.2.16 is this exact example; TJ Appendix D uses x / 2 * Math.PI.

paper_support.quote: The order of operands and operators is wrong.
paper_support.comment: Paper example is result -= a,c; meant as result = a - c. The node's G * m1 * m2 / r * r example comes from S&W Exercise 1.2.7, not from the paper.

paper_support.quote: Wrong order in logical or arithmetic operations.

external_validation.name: Wrong order in logical or arithmetic operations.

misconceptions_and_errors.label: ZeroDivisionAlwaysCrashes
misconceptions_and_errors.wrong_belief: Dividing by zero always stops the program with an error.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule: Only integer division by zero generates a run-time exception; 1.0/0.0 is legal and has the value Infinity.
misconceptions_and_errors.note: Book 1.2 Web Exercise 8 contrasts int and double division by zero.

book_support.quote: The first generates a run-time exception for division by zero (which stops your program because the value is undefined); the second is legal and has the value Infinity.
The result of a calculation can be one of the special values Infinity (if the number is too large to be represented) or NaN (if the result of the calculation is undefined).

misconceptions_and_errors.book_note: The books show 1.0/0.0 = Infinity and Math.sqrt(-1.0) = NaN; the 17.0 % 0.0 = NaN case is correct Java but not in the books.
misconceptions_and_errors.correct_rule_previous: Only int division by zero throws; 17.0 / 0.0 is Infinity and 17.0 % 0.0 is NaN.

final_check.note: '17.0 % 0.0 is NaN' is not in the book.

Values, variables and expressions are written as statements inside main, so a learner must know where statements go and in what order they run before reasoning about values.
edges.literature_note: Knowledge of basics and data sits at the bottom of the skill hierarchy.

edges.logic: A condition is a boolean expression built by comparing typed values, so conditionals use the types, operators and expressions of the previous section.
edges.literature_note: Boolean expressions are rated a core CS1 concept that conditionals depend on.

edges.logic: Arrays are processed by loops whose loop variable serves as the index, so array traversal depends on loop control.
edges.literature_note: Iterative tracing precedes explaining; arrays are processed with index loops.

edges.logic: Input arrives as text that must be converted into typed values, and output turns typed values back into text.
edges.literature_note: Command-line args are Strings that must be parsed into numbers.

edges.logic: The random surfer stores its transition matrix in a 2-D array and its visit counts in a 1-D array.
edges.literature_note: The transition matrix is a 2-D array.

edges.logic: The random surfer is a loop of random moves, with nested loops to build and normalise the matrix.
edges.literature_note: The simulation repeats random moves in a loop.

edges.logic: The random surfer reads its link graph from standard input and writes the page ranks to standard output.
edges.literature_note: Input is n followed by pairs of links.

edges.logic: The source file Name.java holds the public class, and that class must be named Name.
edges.literature_note: The file name is the program name followed by .java.

book_support.quote: Each Java program must reside in a file whose name matches the one after the word class on the first line, and it also must have a .java extension.

edges.book_note: The file-naming rule is stated in terms of the class name; SW p16 also ties the class HelloWorld to the file HelloWorld.java.

final_check.note: SW p17 states the file/class naming rule directly.

edges.logic: main is written inside the class's braces, so java Name looks inside the class Name to find main.

book_support.quote: PROGRAM 1.1.1 consists of a single class named HelloWorld that has a single method named main().
the system calls the main() method that you defined in that class

final_check.note: Both quotes place main() inside the class and say the system calls main() defined in that class.

edges.logic: Statements are written in main's body, and running the program executes main's statements in order, one by one.
edges.literature_note: Sequential execution of statements is among the three most common misconceptions (M23).

book_support.quote: The first line of a method specifies its name and other information; the rest is a sequence of statements enclosed in braces and each followed by a semicolon.
Thus, typing java HelloWorld causes the system to call on the main() method in PROGRAM 1.1.1 and execute its two statements.
ments in order, one by one

edges.book_note: 'Statements run only from inside main' is too strong: any method body holds statements (SW 2.1); in Chapter 1 all statements are in main.
edges.logic_previous: Statements run only from inside main, starting with main's first statement and continuing in order.

final_check.note: 'in order, one by one' is not in the quoted text; it is on the same page: SW p17 'ments in order, one by one' (verify: exact). Add that quote.

edges.logic: A statement block is a sequence of statements, each terminated by a semicolon, enclosed in braces; the body of main() is such a sequence.
edges.literature_note: Students misidentify which statements belong to a body (body boundaries).

book_support.quote: <statements> represents a statement block (a sequence of Java statements, each terminated by a semicolon).
the rest is a sequence of statements enclosed in braces

edges.logic_previous: A block is a list of statements inside { } that run in order as one unit.

final_check.note: Quote (SW p56, section 1.3) says nothing about braces or 'one unit'; braces come from SW p16 'the rest is a sequence of statements enclosed in braces'. The term 'statement block' is first defined in 1.3 (pdf 56).

edges.logic: System.out.print(s); is itself a statement, so it runs at its own place in the sequence of statements.
edges.literature_note: Sequentiality of statements (M23).

ments in order, one by one

ments in order, one by one

edges.logic: java Name runs the Name.class file that javac produced, so compiling must succeed before the program can run.
edges.literature_note: Compile-time errors are caught when compiling, run-time errors when executing.

book_support.quote: Once you compile the program, you can run it.
If there are no errors, the compiler saves the byte code in the file Hello.class. To run the program, the programmer uses java to interpret the byte code.

contrast.logic: javac checks and translates the whole program before it runs (compile-time errors); java executes it and can still fail on particular inputs (run-time errors).

sources.quote: Once you compile the program, you can run it.
To run the program, the programmer uses java to interpret the byte code.

contrast.why_not_parallel: compile is a prerequisite of run; a parallel edge would put both on one path

final_check.note: SW p15 + TJ p28 support compile-before-run and the .class file.

edges.logic: A literal is the source-code form of a value of some type, and the way it is written fixes that type: 1234 is an int, 3.14 a double, true a boolean, 'c' a char.
edges.literature_note: Data-type knowledge sits at the base of the hierarchy.

book_support.quote: A literal is a source-code representation of a data-type value.
We use strings of digits like 1234 or 99 to define int literal values, and add a decimal point as in 3.14159 or 2.71828 to define double literal values.

edges.book_note: Logic says "every literal has a primitive type", but "Hello" is a String literal (SW p25), and String is not primitive.
edges.logic_previous: Every literal has a primitive type fixed by how it is written: a whole number is an int, a number with a decimal point is a double, true or false is a boolean, and 'c' is a char.

final_check.note: Definition + int/double literal forms quoted; boolean ('keywords true or false', p25) and char (p29 'Literals for char are characters enclosed in') are on other lines, faithful.

edges.logic: A variable of type t is given a value of type t, often written as a literal.
edges.book_note: SW p25 defines a variable as "a name that we use to refer to a data-type value", without using literals; literals only appear as the values assigned in the example (int a, b, c; a = 1234; ...). The dependency is weak: a variable can get its value from any expression.

final_check.note: order_only. Nearest SW support: p25 'using the literals 1234 and 99' (assignment statements change variables using literals) - supports literal->assignment rather than literal->variable.

edges.logic: Assignment needs a declared variable on its left side to store the computed value into.
edges.literature_note: Variable and assignment models are studied together; assignment needs the variable concept.

book_support.quote: The left-hand side of an assignment statement must be a single variable; the right-hand side can be an arbitrary expression that produces values of the type.

final_check.note: 'declared' is supported by SW p26 'Declarations can ... appear anywhere before a variable is first used'.

edges.logic: An expression can be a literal, a variable, or operations on them; we compute with a variable by using its name in an expression.
edges.literature_note: In x = x + k, x on the right means the current value.

book_support.quote: An expression is a literal, a variable, or a
sequence of operations on literals and/or variables that produces a value.
We compute with it by using the name in an expression that uses operations defined for its type.
A variable is a name that we use to refer to a data-type value

edges.logic_previous: When a variable x appears in an expression, Java uses the value x holds at that moment.

final_check.note: 'the value x holds at that moment' is not in the quotes; SW p25 'A variable is a name that we use to refer to a data-type value.' is the closest support.

edges.logic: An operator combines operand values a and b into a new value, so operators build larger expressions from smaller ones.

book_support.quote: For primitive types, expressions look just like mathematical formulas, which are based on familiar symbols or operators that specify data-type operations to be performed on one or more operands.

edges.book_note: Expression (pdf 27) is defined with generic operators such as x + 1 and y / 2; the full int operator set comes at pdf 31.

final_check.note: Faithful; SW p27 also says 'Each operand can be any expression.' (verify: exact).

edges.logic: For ints a and b, / gives the whole quotient q and % gives the remainder r, so that a = b * q + r.
edges.literature_note: TargetTyping: an int / int expression has type int.

book_support.quote: given two int values a and b, the value of a / b is the number of times b goes into a with the fractional part discarded, and the value of a % b is the remainder that you get when you divide a by b.
(a / b) * b + a % b is always equal to a

edges.logic: Both come from finite representations: an int result too large for 32 bits wraps around silently (overflow), while a double keeps about 15 significant digits so most results are approximations (5.0/3.0 is 1.6666666666666667). Neither raises an error.

edges.guards_against: expecting Java to report arithmetic that does not fit, or doubles to be exact

edges.logic: Both make one pass over the values with one variable kept across passes. book_support.quote: double max = Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY; for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) if (a[i] > max) max = a[i];
double sum = 0.0; for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sum += a[i];

[pseudocode] bubble sort used for the SOLO descriptor table
for i <- 2 to N do
  for j <- N downto i do
    if (array[j] < array[j-1]) then
      temp <- array[j]
      array[j] <- array[j-1]
      array[j-1] <- temp
    end if
  end for
end for

[pseudocode] extended-abstract example: early exit with a flag
i <- 2
do
  AscendingOrder <- True
  for j = N downto i do
    if (number[j] < number[j-1]) then
      swap(number[j], number[j-1])
      AscendingOrder <- False
    end if
  end for
  i <- i + 1
while not AscendingOrder
literature_content.note: Bubble-sort EA example.
